walkthroughs.body_html:
Foundations in Chemistry — a core area of A-Level Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Foundations in Chemistry brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Foundations in Chemistry.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Members of a homologous series share:
options: The same molecular mass
The same functional group and general formula
The same boiling point
The same number of isomers

mcqs.q: When you reverse a reaction in a Hess cycle, what happens to ΔH?
options: Its sign reverses — if the forward reaction is +100 kJ/mol, the reverse is -100 kJ/mol.
The fingerprint region is the part that contains all the most useful absorptions.
ΔH stays the same because it's the same reaction.
ΔH becomes zero because the change cancels out.

mcqs.q: When an acid neutralises an alkali, what is the pH of the resulting solution?
options: Approximately 7 if equivalent amounts of strong acid and strong alkali react — but it varies with strength.
Neutralisation always produces a solution with pH exactly 7 regardless of the acid and base used.
Neutralisation always produces a solution with pH 0.
ΔH becomes zero because the change cancels out.

mcqs.q: What is the role of the fingerprint region (below ~1500 cm^-1) in IR spectroscopy?
options: The fingerprint region is the part that contains all the most useful absorptions.
ΔH becomes zero because the change cancels out.
The fingerprint region is used to identify which functional groups are present.
It is unique to each compound — used to identify a specific molecule by matching to a known spectrum.
